Product Image Source Comparison for Planogram and SKU Recognition

Goal: polished ecommerce product photos, packaged retail SKU front images, consistent lighting/backgrounds, and clean label shots for planograms.

Best GS1 / GDSN Standardized front, side, top, back, right, and bottom views. Best fit for planograms when you can access the data pool.
Best Brand / Manufacturer Clean official packshots. Often excellent for exact SKU recognition, but rights must be checked.
Useful Retailer PDP High-quality images from ecommerce pages. Usually restricted by terms, so treat as reference unless licensed.
Mixed Open Food Facts Broad package coverage and API access, but image quality is inconsistent and license obligations apply.
Poor Fit USDA Good public-domain agriculture images, but not clean packaged retail SKU packshots.
GS1 is mostly a standard and data-exchange ecosystem, not a free public catalog. The GS1 examples below show the type of SKU image you should request or acquire: {GTIN}.1 for front planogram image, {GTIN}.2 for left, {GTIN}.3 for top, {GTIN}.7 for back, {GTIN}.8 for right, and {GTIN}.9 for bottom.

Overall Source Comparison

Source Planogram Fit Image Quality Commercial Risk What to Do for Commercial Use Best Use Reference
GS1 / GDSN High High Not automatically free; access/licensing required Use a licensed GDSN/data-pool feed, get brand permission, or create your own GS1-standard photos. Planograms, front/side/top SKU assets, shelf simulation, retailer-ready product data. GS1 Product Image Specification
Brand / Manufacturer High High Depends on permission Request written permission, a media-kit license, or a brand product-content feed. Exact SKU front images, product recognition, catalog matching. Official brand product pages and press/media kits.
Retailer PDP High High Terms often restrict reuse Do not scrape for production unless terms/license allow it; prefer retailer API, affiliate/feed agreement, or brand source. Reference matching, internal experiments, visual QA if licensed or allowed. Retailer product detail pages.
Open Food Facts Medium Mixed CC BY-SA obligations Follow attribution/share-alike requirements and track source URLs/barcodes for every image. Barcode lookup, broad coverage, bootstrapping product recognition. Open Food Facts API
USDA Low Good for agriculture Often public domain Confirm the exact USDA image says public domain/copyright-free; avoid USDA logos or implied endorsement. Agriculture/food category imagery, not packaged SKU packshots. USDA ARS image copyright

Commercial Use Checklist

Source Can You Use Commercially? What You Should Do What to Avoid
GS1 / GDSN Yes, only with proper access/license. GS1 standards are usable, but GS1-style product images are not automatically free. Get a licensed data-pool/product-content feed, ask the brand for rights, or photograph/render your own images using GS1 rules. Do not download random product images and assume they are commercially usable because they follow GS1 naming or style.
Brand / Manufacturer Yes, if the brand grants rights or the media kit explicitly allows the use. Ask for written approval for your use case: ML training, planogram rendering, ecommerce display, redistribution, or app screenshots. Do not republish brand images publicly without permission, especially in paid products or customer-facing demos.
Retailer PDP Usually risky unless licensed. Retailer terms often restrict scraping and reuse. Use official APIs, partner feeds, affiliate/product feeds, or switch to brand/GDSN assets for production. Do not scrape retailer pages for a commercial dataset without reviewing terms and rights.
Open Food Facts Possible, but license obligations apply. Keep attribution, product URL/barcode, contributor/license records, and comply with CC BY-SA/share-alike requirements. Do not mix Open Food Facts images into a closed proprietary image set unless your legal/license plan handles share-alike.
USDA Often yes for USDA-created public-domain images, but check each image. Verify the exact page says public domain/copyright-free, credit USDA when requested, and avoid endorsement claims. Do not use USDA logos/seals or make it look like USDA endorses your product.
